sections.body:
A **fruit salad** is fruit that has been cut up and mixed together in one bowl. That is all it is. Some fruit salads are simple, with just two or three fruits. Some have ten.

Fruit is good for you because it has **vitamins**. Vitamins are tiny helpers your body needs. They help you see, help you fight germs, and help you grow. They are a bit like tiny builders working inside you.

Fruit also has **fibre**, which keeps your tummy happy. And it has water, so it helps you feel fresh on a hot day.

Different fruits have different colours, and the colour tells you something. Red and pink fruits, like watermelon and strawberry, are rich in a vitamin called **vitamin C**. Orange and yellow fruits, like mango and papaya, are rich in **vitamin A**, which helps your eyes. Green fruits, like kiwi and guava, are full of vitamins and fibre too.

A fruit salad is a great way to eat many fruits at once. Each colour gives you something different. That is why a bowl with many colours is usually the best bowl.

Fruit salad is also a food you can **make yourself**. With a knife, a board and a bowl, you can make it in ten minutes.
examples: A fruit salad is cut fruit mixed in a bowl.
Watermelon is red, so it has lots of vitamin C.
I made a fruit salad with mango and papaya.
sections.heading: What a fruit salad is

sections.body:
Not every fruit likes every other fruit. Some pairs are wonderful. Some pairs taste strange. Here are some good rules and some good pairs.

Sweet with sharp is a great match. A sweet mango and a sharp lime or a sour passion fruit wake each other up.

Soft with crunchy is also lovely. A soft banana beside a crunchy apple makes your mouth happy.

Same family, same colour is safe and always works. Melon with melon, or berries with berries.

Watch out for two things. **Banana and pineapple** together can taste a bit odd, because pineapple is sharp and kills the smell of banana. **Papaya and kiwi** together can taste a bit soapy, so many people keep them apart.

Citrus fruit, like oranges and mandarins, has a thin skin and no seeds. It is easy and sweet. **Melons** have a thick skin and lots of seeds, so they need an adult to cut them.

And here is a very useful tip. Add the **soft fruit last**. Cut the hard fruit first and put it in the bowl. Cut the banana and the mango last, just before you eat. Soft fruit turns to mush if it sits for a long time, while hard fruit keeps its shape for hours.
examples: Sweet mango and sharp lime taste great together.
I add the banana last so it does not go mushy.
We keep papaya and kiwi in separate bowls.
sections.heading: Choosing fruits that taste good together

sections.body:
You do not need many things to make a fruit salad. Here is what to ask a grown-up for.

A **knife** for cutting. A **chopping board** so the knife does not slip. A **big bowl** to mix everything. A **spoon** to stir. And a **colander** or a sieve for washing the fruit under running water.

Now the safety part, and this part really matters.

Always cut fruit on a board, never in the air, and never while holding it in your hand. A fruit that slips is a cut hand.

Use the right knife for the job. A **peeler** takes the skin off apples and carrots. A **grater** makes small pieces. A **knife** does the rest.

Fruit can have **stones** or **pits** inside. Peaches, plums, mangoes and cherries all have one. Never cut a stone with the knife pointing towards you. Ask an adult to take the stones out.

Wash every piece of fruit under running water, even the ones you are going to peel. The dirt on the outside can go to the inside on the knife.

And wash your hands, tie your hair back, and take small steps. A fruit salad is easy.
examples: I ask for a knife, a board and a big bowl.
I wash the fruit under the tap before I cut it.
An adult takes the stones out of the peaches.
sections.heading: The tools you need, and how to stay safe

sections.body:
These are the words for the things in your bowl and the things you do to them.

To **slice** is to cut into thin flat pieces. You slice a banana.

To **dice** is to cut into small cubes. You dice the mango.

To **peel** is to take the skin off. You peel a mango with a peeler or a spoon.

Juice is the water inside a fruit. You can squeeze lemon juice over the salad.

Pip or **seed** is the small hard thing inside a fruit. You take the pips out.

A **core** is the hard middle of an apple or a pear, with the seeds inside it.

To **chill** is to make something cold. A chilled fruit salad tastes the best.
examples: To slice means to cut thin flat pieces.
To dice means to cut small cubes.
We chill the salad so it tastes fresh.
sections.heading: The fruit words, one by one

terms.example: I slice the banana and put it on top.
terms.gloss: To cut something into thin, flat pieces.

terms.example: Please dice the mango for the salad.
terms.gloss: To cut something into small cubes.

terms.example: Dad peels the papaya with a spoon.
terms.gloss: To take the skin off a fruit or vegetable.

terms.example: I squeeze some lime juice over the fruit.
terms.gloss: The liquid water inside a fruit.

terms.example: We chill the salad in the fridge for one hour.
terms.gloss: To make something cold so it tastes fresh.

sections.body:
This recipe makes four big bowls of fruit salad. It is easy and it is fun. Ask a grown-up to help with the knife and the knife-sharp stone fruit.

You need one apple, one pear, one mango, two bananas, a few strawberries, and a little lime or lemon juice. The lime keeps the apple from turning brown, and it makes the whole bowl taste fresher.
examples: First I wash all the fruit.
Then I dice the apple and the pear.
Last I add the banana, just before we eat.
sections.heading: How to make a fruit salad
steps: Wash all the fruit under running water.
Peel and core the apple and pear, then dice them into the big bowl.
Peel and dice the mango, and put it in the bowl.
Slice the strawberries and add them.
Squeeze in a little lime juice, then stir gently.
Slice the bananas and add them just before you eat. Then chill the bowl for one hour.

sections.body:
Fruit salad looks beautiful in a glass bowl. Put a big spoon in it and let everyone help themselves.

You can serve it three ways. **Straight**, cold from the fridge, with nothing on it. **With yoghurt**, so you scoop cold creamy yoghurt over the fruit. Or **as a drink**, blended with a little milk or ice into a smoothie.

Some fruit salads get watery as they sit. If you make too much, keep it in a covered bowl in the fridge and eat it the next day. If the bottom of the bowl gets watery, use a colander to drain the fruit before serving.

Now try these sentences. They work at home, at a party, or at school.

If someone asks why fruit is good for you, say it has vitamins and fibre, and that the different colours give different vitamins.

And if you are proud of your bowl, say it plainly. You made it, and it looks lovely.
examples: I made this fruit salad all by myself.
Fruit has vitamins and fibre, so it is good for you.
We are serving the salad with yoghurt tonight.
The salad is best cold from the fridge.
sections.heading: Serving it and saying it out loud

item.summary: A fruit salad is fruit, cut up and mixed. After reading this you can choose fruits that taste good together, cut fruit safely, make a simple fruit salad at home, and name the colours and vitamins you are eating.
item.title: Let's Make a Fruit Salad
